exercises.objective: Apply Sylvester's criterion to determine whether candidate metric tensors are valid.
exercises.prompt: Two candidate metric tensors are proposed: $G_1=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and $G_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$. Using Sylvester's criterion, determine which (if either) is a valid metric tensor (i.e. positive definite), and explain what goes wrong for the invalid one.
hints: Sylvester's criterion for a 2x2 symmetric matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&d\end{pmatrix}$: PD iff $a>0$ and $ad-b^2>0$.

For $G_2$: $a=1>0$, but $ad-b^2=1(1)-2^2=1-4=-3<0$. So $G_1$ is valid (PD); $G_2$ is not (you can even find a specific $v$ with $v^\top G_2v<0$, e.g. $v=(1,-1)$: $v^\top G_2v = 1-2-2+1=-2<0$, confirming it directly).

exercises.objective: Compute a scalar product using a non-orthonormal metric tensor.
exercises.prompt: Let $G=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ (first confirm to yourself this is a valid PD metric tensor via Sylvester's criterion), $v=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$, $w=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\end{pmatrix}$. Compute $\langle v,w\rangle = v^\top Gw$. Enter a decimal.

exercises.objective: Derive the orthogonal projection matrix onto the span of orthonormal vectors, and prove idempotency.
exercises.prompt: Let $\{e_1,..,e_k\}$ be orthonormal (w.r.t. the standard dot product), and let $U=[e_1\;\cdots\;e_k]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$. Starting from the projection formula $P(x)=\sum_{i=1}^ke_i\langle e_i,x\rangle$, (a) show that $P(x) = UU^\top x$, i.e. that the projection is the linear map with matrix $P=UU^\top$. (b) Prove that $P$ is idempotent, $P^2=P$ (a defining property of any projection: projecting twice does nothing more than projecting once).
hints: For (a): $\langle e_i,x\rangle = e_i^\top x$ for the standard dot product, a scalar. So $e_i\langle e_i,x\rangle = e_i(e_i^\top x) = (e_ie_i^\top)x$. Summing over $i$: $P(x)=\sum_ie_ie_i^\top x = \left(\sum_ie_ie_i^\top\right)x$. Recognize $\sum_ie_ie_i^\top = UU^\top$ (this is exactly what the matrix product $UU^\top$ computes when $U$'s columns are the $e_i$).
For (b): $P^2 = (UU^\top)(UU^\top) = U(U^\top U)U^\top$. What is $U^\top U$, given the $e_i$ are orthonormal?

$U^\top U = I_k$ (the $(i,j)$ entry of $U^\top U$ is $e_i^\top e_j=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$, exactly the identity matrix). So $P^2 = U I_kU^\top = UU^\top = P$. Idempotency confirmed: geometrically, once you've projected onto the span, projecting again changes nothing, you're already there.
